So let's start. E-safety, or online safety, is the safe, responsible and ethical use of technology.
That includes the internet, text messages, messaging apps, online gaming, email and smart connected devices.
And it isn't just common sense stuff. E-safety is as much about behaviour as it is about security. How you treat others, what you share, and who you trust.
Privacy means keeping control of your personal information and who can see it. And online, a secret can spread much faster and further than in the playground.
Some facts from the book. Nearly one in three eleven to thirteen year olds have broadcast themselves live on the internet.
Eighty-one percent of eight to seventeen year olds say they know how to ask permission before posting something about someone else.
But fifty-two percent say someone shared a photo or video of them without asking.

So, why should you always ask before posting a photo of a friend? It's their image, they might be embarrassed or upset, it could reveal personal information like their school uniform, and once it's posted, you can't take it back.
Page two: personal information. That's information that could identify you, or help someone find or contact you.
The golden rule: keep it private. Your home address, phone number, email address, date of birth, full name, school, and photos of you.
Even your age and how many brothers and sisters you have count as personal information.
Pause and test yourself. Which is riskier to share: your favourite video game genre, or a photo of you in your E R G S uniform?
The uniform photo is high risk. The badge shows which school you go to, so someone could find you there. Your favourite game genre is low risk.
Though groomers can use shared interests to build trust, so even that needs a bit of care.
High risk items also include your home address, your mobile number, your date of birth with your full name, and a live geotagged status update, which shows exactly where you are right now.
Before you share anything, ask: could a stranger use this to find me, contact me, or pretend to be me? If yes, keep it private.
And small pieces add up. Your first name, plus your football club, plus a photo outside your house, can be pieced together to find you.
Page three is a true or false round, based on Becky's story. Aoife, true or false: it's okay to post a photo of yourself in your school uniform.
False. Photos online are there forever, and your uniform shows your school. And use an avatar, which is a cool graphic, instead of your own photo as a profile picture.
True or false: it's okay to accept friends you don't know in person.
False. The average person has around fifty-five real-life friends but over two hundred online friends. And adults with bad intentions can pretend to be young people.
True or false: it's okay to post when you go on holiday.
False. You've just told everyone your house is empty. Post your holiday photos after you get home.
And true or false: it's a good idea to keep your profile private.
True! Privacy settings mean only your real friends see what you post.

Page four: online gaming. That means playing in real time with people across the world.
Ninety-one percent of children are gamers. And sixty-eight point eight percent of Fortnite players have spent money on in-game purchases.
The risks are offensive chat, strangers, in-game purchases that run up big bills, and griefing.
Griefing means deliberately spoiling other players' games through harassment or cheating.
To stay safe: tell your parents who you play with. Use appropriate language, and learn how to report and block.
Use airplane mode for offline games on a phone or tablet, ask a parent to set up purchase controls, keep gaming friends in the game, and never agree to meet someone you only know from a game.
In the book, Ryan, who's twelve, is offered free V Bucks by a player who says he's thirteen, and then asks for Ryan's Snapchat.
Free gifts and moving quickly to a private app are warning signs. Ryan should say no, keep chat in the game, and tell a trusted adult.
Page five: downloading. Downloading films, music and games is useful, but files from illegal or unknown sites can carry malware.
Malware is short for malicious software, the name for all harmful programs. Let's go through them.
A virus is harmful code that attaches to genuine programs, copies itself, and corrupts or deletes files.
A trojan is malware disguised as something you want, like a free game mod, that secretly opens a back door so attackers can get in.
A worm spreads itself from computer to computer across a network, slowing everything down.
Spyware and keyloggers secretly watch what you do and record your key presses, to steal passwords and bank details.
Phishing is fake emails or messages pretending to be a real organisation, to trick you into giving away details.
Pharming secretly redirects you from a real website to a fake copy, to capture your login details.
And copyright infringement is illegally downloading or sharing music, films or software, which breaks UK copyright law.

Page six: social networks. They let you stay in touch, meet people with similar interests, and share your creativity.
But the minimum age for most of them is thirteen. That includes Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube accounts and X, formerly Twitter.
There are three settings to check on every app. Privacy settings, set to the strongest level. Tag approvals, so you approve tags before they appear on your profile.
And location services. Turn them off so people can't see where you are. On Snapchat's Snap Map, use Ghost Mode.
Risks include information being copied and spread, posts that are hard to take back, strangers, and chatrooms that aren't moderated, which are places groomers go to contact children.
Page seven: cyberbullying. That's bullying others using electronic devices, like social media, messaging, phones or gaming platforms. It's usually repeated and deliberate.

It's different from other bullying because it can happen twenty-four seven, it follows you home through your phone, it can reach a huge audience instantly, it's often anonymous, and it can escalate as others join in.
The forms include threats and intimidation, harassment and stalking, and defamation, which is spreading untrue rumours that damage someone's reputation.
Also rejection and exclusion, like deliberately leaving someone out of group chats. Identity theft and impersonation. And sharing someone's private information or photos.
And a troll is someone who deliberately posts inflammatory comments, to start arguments and upset people.
But bullies can be caught. Every device online has an I P address, which the police and C E O P can use to trace where bullying came from, even when it's anonymous.
In the book, pupils keep posting a photo of Emma with mean comments, and remove her from the group chat. Is it cyberbullying?
Yes. It's on a device, it's repeated, and it's deliberate. Emma should keep screenshots and tell a trusted adult.
Page eight: grooming. Online grooming is when someone befriends a young person and builds an emotional connection, to lower their guard so they can exploit or abuse them.
Groomers often use fake profiles and pretend to be young. They offer gifts like game currency, give lots of compliments, and pretend to share your interests.
Then they try to move the chat to private messaging, ask for photos, or try to set up a meeting.
And groomers are not always strangers. Sometimes they're people already known through family or activities.
The crucial rule: never agree to meet an online contact in person, and never send photos to someone you don't know. Once sent, you lose control of it forever.
If you're ever worried, tell a trusted adult. A parent, guardian, form tutor, Head of Year, or the school's Designated Teacher for Child Protection.
Inappropriate content means anything upsetting, meant for adults, untrue, or that might tempt you into dangerous or illegal behaviour.
If you see something that upsets you, close it, don't share it, and tell a trusted adult. It is never your fault.
Page nine: your digital footprint. That's the trail left behind by all your interactions using the internet, email, social media, texting and more. And it's often permanent.
Test yourself. You have two hundred online friends, and each of them has five hundred friends. How many people are friends of your friends?
Two hundred times five hundred is one hundred thousand people. And friends of friends of friends? Fifty million.
That's over twenty-five times the population of Northern Ireland. Real numbers are smaller because friend groups overlap, but the point stands.
Your digital reputation is how people see you because of your behaviour and posts online. A poor one can affect friendships and even job prospects.
So think before you post. T H I N K. Is it True? Is it Helpful? Is it Inspiring? Is it Necessary? Is it Kind?

One: don't delete the messages. Screenshots are evidence.
Two: don't reply or retaliate. It makes things worse.
Three: tell a trusted adult straight away.

Let's recap. E-safety is the safe and responsible use of technology. Keep personal information private, and remember small details add up.
Only accept friends you know in real life, keep your profile private, and turn off location services.
Malware includes viruses, trojans, worms and spyware. Phishing uses fake messages, pharming uses fake websites.
Cyberbullying is repeated, deliberate harm using devices. Never meet an online contact, and never send photos to strangers.
Your digital footprint is often permanent, so think before you post.
And if something worries you: don't delete, don't reply, tell a trusted adult, and report it.
